--- title: 'PE100-09: Strings' --- We've been using strings in each of the previous modules, but we've accepted them as a found artifact without really getting into them and seeing how they. This module will correct that deficiency and make all of us better ~~people~~ programmers. ### Review time Let's take a quick look at what we've done so far. ``` String literals: "Doug McKenzie" String variables: comedic_genius = "Mel Brooks" Comparison: if my_name == your_name: if your_name != "Chuck Woolery": Concatenation: full_name = first_name+last_name Repetition: "ABC" * 20 ``` There is a lot more we can do with strings. We can: * Index into them * Iterate over them * Slice them * Search them * Call methods that act on them... In fact, when you look at what you can do with a string and how you do it, you suddenly realize that a string is just (conceptually) a tuple of letters. We can index into a string: ::: {#4bb82943-bca0-4f08-a1c0-ddae813a6692 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} my_name="John Belushi" print(my_name[0]) print(my_name[len(my_name)-1]) print(my_name[-1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` J i i ``` ::: ::: Strings are iterables: ::: {#31c6e197-4fee-4c2b-833b-12b67db3ff4b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} for char in my_name: print(char) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` J o h n B e l u s h i ``` ::: ::: Just like a tuple, the elements of a string are immutable. Once a string is created, the characters can't be changed. ::: {#5f7d5ca5-2326-4c00-aebe-22af4501572b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} my_name="Bob" my_name[0]='R' ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}
